According to the first, Byzantium had already become a feudal society beginning in the fifth century. By the seventh century, this system had become firmly established and the slave economy was approaching its end.
According to the second theory, the slave economy was still declining during the fifth to seventh centuries, while the feudal economy was only slowly taking shape.

The Soviet Orientalist Belyaev, for his part, argues that modern research into the use of slaves in agriculture, irrigation and different crafts shows that slave ownership was also a feature of feudal society in the Byzantine Empire and the Middle East.
He therefore takes feudalism to have been the dominant system in the territories ruled by Byzantium.
When discussing the social and economic relations and property laws of the countries conquered by the Arabs more generally, he likewise speaks of “the feudal system that was widespread there.”
This includes both the regions previously ruled by the Sasanians and those previously ruled by Byzantium.

Elsewhere in his book, when speaking specifically about former Sasanian societies, Belyaev likewise treats their feudal character as an established fact rather than something requiring further argument.
The Arab-Islamic society that emerged during the early conquests, however, was far from uniform.
As Belyaev describes it, the social and economic relations and property laws of the conquered countries were new and unfamiliar to the Arab conquerors.
The feudal system widespread in those regions did not interest them. Nor were they initially interested in owning the land, which they regarded as the common property of the Muslims.

As a result, “the land remained in the hands of the local feudal lords, chiefs, religious authorities and other owners. The landowners kept their full rights and privileges and continued to exploit the peasants as they had before...”
At the same time, “the tribal and clan organization retained by the Arabs in the conquered countries prevented them from mixing with the conquered peoples...”
Belyaev nevertheless regards the Umayyad period as “a distinctive period in Arab history.”

One of the main reasons, in his view, was “the social and economic changes that took place in the caliphate under the Umayyads and led to the victory of feudal relations among the peoples of the Arab state, including the Arabs themselves.”

Even then, however, Belyaev believes that the final victory of these relations came only in the ninth century CE, when “the caliphate in Baghdad became a feudal state” and “the role of slaves in production declined.”

We also find another contemporary Marxist thinker who dealt with the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage in a work on medieval philosophy. He argues that when Islam emerged, feudal relations of production finally replaced slave-based relations of production. At the same time, he says that the particular nature of this feudal system still needs detailed study from a Marxist point of view.

The first Marxist Orientalist studies of Arab-Islamic philosophy focused on the progressive role played by Islamic thinkers and philosophers in developing a culture that reflected the material and intellectual rise of the progressive class forces within Arab-Islamic society under the Abbasid Caliphate.

Among the leading scholars in this field were Yakubovsky; Sadriddin Ayni, the former president of the Academy of Sciences of Soviet Tajikistan; Ghafurov, director of the Institute of Oriental Studies in Moscow, formerly the Institute of Asia and Africa; Krachkovsky; Bartold; Krymsky; and Grigoryev.

Another feature of these studies is that they approached the intellectual heritage through scientific interpretation. On the hundredth anniversary of the birth of the Russian Orientalist Gordlevsky, an important study of his in this field appeared in Moscow as part of his collected works.

In 1939, the Soviet Union published a History of Philosophy containing a study of Arab-Islamic philosophy written from a materialist standpoint. Another work with the same title, History of Philosophy, was published in six volumes by the Soviet Academy of Philosophical Sciences and included a study of the historical development of Arab-Islamic philosophy.

In more recent years, Soviet Oriental studies began to examine particular questions within this philosophy in a more specialized way. There were also university dissertations in philosophy, such as A. S. Ivanov’s study, “Al-Fārābī’s Teaching on the Human Capacity for Knowledge.”

Other specialized studies included a commentary on al-Fārābī’s treatise What Must Precede the Study of Philosophy, published in The Philosophical Treatises of al-Fārābī in Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan, in 1970; “The Problem of Sensory Knowledge in the Treatises of al-Fārābī,” based on papers from the scientific conference of young researchers at the Academy of Sciences of Soviet Kazakhstan, also published in Alma-Ata in 1970; “Al-Fārābī’s Theory of Knowledge,” published by the Social Sciences Division of the Kazakh Academy of Sciences in 1971; Al-Fārābī in Historical Scholarship, published in Alma-Ata in 1971; and “Some Questions Concerning al-Fārābī’s Philosophical Heritage,” included in the book Al-Fārābī: A Great Scholar of Encyclopedic Knowledge.

Several studies on different aspects of Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy were also published in Tashkent, the capital of Soviet Uzbekistan. A Russian-language book entitled Monuments of Arab Thought appeared with philosophical texts and commentaries. And in Moscow, during the past two years, the academic philosopher L. Sagadeev published two works, one on Ibn Sīnā and the other on Ibn Rushd.

Some earlier Soviet works also took a clear stand against Eurocentrism in philosophy. They supported, on the one hand, the idea that world philosophy forms a single whole and, on the other, the idea that different local philosophies have their own distinctive features, shaped by their particular national and historical conditions.
We can see the main direction of these Soviet studies in the following examples.

The Soviet historian Bukhonsky writes that, for Ibn Sīnā, knowledge is based on our perception of things that exist outside us and independently of us. He says that Ibn Sīnā does not doubt the objectivity of knowledge or the importance of rational thought. In this sense, Ibn Sīnā is an opponent of irrationalism.

Bukhonsky also argues that Ibn Sīnā changed Aristotle’s concept of “form” in a way that brought a material principle into the explanation of the individual, particular thing. Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy also accepts the eternity of the world. This, Bukhonsky argues, reduces the weight of the theological and idealist elements found in Ibn Sīnā’s teaching on the soul.
Finally, Bukhonsky stresses that Ibn Sīnā dealt with questions of logic independently of Aristotle.

The Soviet historian of philosophy Trachtenberg wrote a book entitled A Sketch of the History of Western Europe in the Middle Ages. A very large part of it is devoted to Arab-Islamic philosophy. Among the conclusions he reaches are the following.

On the Muʿtazila, he argues that their central concept was reason. Their belief that God creates the world continuously, through an endlessly renewed act of creation, leads in his view to the eternity of the material world. If creation is continuous, the argument goes, then if the world came to an end, God too would come to an end. The world must therefore be eternal for God to remain eternal. Trachtenberg sees a similarity here with Neoplatonism, which also sees God as continuously active in the universe in order to preserve the unity of the world.
On Ibn Rushd, Trachtenberg argues that Ibn Rushd understands God as the first mover. In this respect, he compares him with Descartes, who also regarded God as the source of motion.

But Ibn Rushd, he says, makes God the source of matter in terms of its end rather than its beginning. In other words, God is matter’s goal. This follows Aristotle’s distinction between an efficient cause, which produces something, and a final cause, which is the end or purpose toward which it moves. For Aristotle, God is a final cause: the ultimate goal of matter’s existence.

Trachtenberg argues that Ibn Rushd tries to explain matter in physical terms. Matter gives form to itself, and living beings arise through heat. When the heat disappears, those living beings disappear as well.

This idea of Ibn Rushd later passed to the Italian philosopher Pietro Pomponazzi (1464–1524), who was executed on the charge of being an Averroist, and to the Italian philosopher Bernardino Telesio (1508–1588), who adopted Ibn Rushd’s view that heat causes non-living matter to become living matter.
For Ibn Rushd, Trachtenberg says, the intellect of the world is a law—a law of necessity. He therefore asks: is the intellect of the world an essence, or is it not?

His answer is that, for Ibn Rushd, it is not an essence but a necessity. Ibn Rushd separates the idea of intellect from the idea of spirit or soul. He says that intellect is present in every existing thing.
The world is therefore intelligible because it follows laws. God does not intervene in its affairs, because the world is intelligible in itself—that is, it is governed by necessity and causation.

In Trachtenberg’s reading, this means that Ibn Rushd rejects al-Ghazālī’s theoretical position. Al-Ghazālī held that when one thing regularly appears together with another, this does not prove that one causes the other. The connection may simply be circumstantial or coincidental, and through repetition it comes to seem habitual. People repeatedly see burning occur when fire comes into contact with matter, for example, and so they come to regard fire as the cause of the burning.

Trachtenberg also sees Ibn Rushd as a materialist in his theory of knowledge. Ibn Rushd, he says, believes that knowledge is acquired when material things act upon our senses. If we add this to his belief in the eternity of matter and his recognition that the material world exists objectively, Trachtenberg argues that there can be no doubt about his materialism.
The world develops on the basis of reason. This too, in Trachtenberg’s view, is a materialist position. But Ibn Rushd’s materialism belongs specifically to the Middle Ages.

As the German historian Lange puts it, medieval materialists became extremely skilled at hiding what they really thought. They could therefore develop materialist ideas while outwardly presenting them in forms that defended religion and theology.

Trachtenberg also sees a similarity between Ibn Rushd and Hegel in the way both reduce God to a “general idea.” The similarity, as he sees it, lies in the fact that for both thinkers reason is a law of necessity. This amounts to recognizing necessity in the world: the world is intelligible because it operates according to rational laws.
Here again, Ibn Rushd recognizes that matter—the world—exists independently of consciousness. In other words, he recognizes the objective existence of the world.

Professor T. Skovsky, in the lectures on the history of philosophy that we mentioned earlier, says that Marxism rejects the claim that Ibn Sīnā, Ibn Rushd, and the other Arab philosophers were simply Peripatetics—followers of Aristotle.

The facts themselves, he argues, support this rejection. The Arab philosophers did not stop with Aristotle’s teaching as they received it. They developed it. Aristotelianism was indeed the basis of their philosophy, but they pushed Aristotle’s teaching in a materialist direction.

Discussing Ibn Sīnā’s logic, Skovsky says that his study of the nature of judgments and logical categories is especially valuable. The strength of Ibn Sīnā’s logic lies in the fact that he examines the actual content of logical categories, one of the most difficult problems in philosophy.

In his logical writings, for example, Ibn Sīnā distinguishes between explaining a certain judgment and explaining an essence. He also defines such categories as affirmation and negation, universal and particular, possibility and actuality. The last two—possibility and actuality—are closely connected with Ibn Sīnā’s metaphysics.

In medieval European philosophy, Skovsky says, one theory dominated: the doctrine that the world had been created out of nothing. Arab philosophers, by contrast, examined every kind of question concerning the world and nature.

Europe did not begin to discuss the problems of nature, or even to ask what nature is, until it became familiar with Ibn Sīnā’s works. From then on, European thinkers began asking questions about living and non-living things, and so on.

Skovsky also argues that Marxist analysis always relates the level reached by science and philosophy to the level of economic development. If we apply this approach to medieval Arab philosophy, he says, we must look at the economy of the Arab countries, which during the period of the conquests had reached a higher level than the economy of Europe.
At that time, many branches of science flourished among the Arabs alongside philosophy. This is only natural, he says: where science flourishes, philosophy flourishes too.
The much greater economic development of the Arab world compared with Europe may therefore have provided the basis for the appearance of materialist tendencies in Arab philosophy.

The German Marxist thinker Hermann Ley, in his Brief History of Materialism in the Middle Ages, which we mentioned earlier, argues that the central idea in Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy is that matter has laws of its own.

In Ley’s view, Ibn Sīnā opposes Platonic idealism, especially the changes that Plotinus introduced into Plato’s teaching. Through this same idea, Ibn Sīnā also moves beyond those parts of Aristotle’s teaching on matter and form that remained close to Plato.

Aristotle believed that the problems of coming into being, change, and passing away in nature could be solved by separating in thought the “form” of a thing from its “matter” and from its external existence. This separation creates a material realm and an intellectual realm, with an idealist division between the two.

Even so, when Aristotle is compared with Plato, Aristotle’s philosophy represents a development in the direction of materialist thought. Aristotle’s criticism of Plato helped open the way toward connecting recognition of the material nature of the world with recognition, at least to some extent, of the material character of the laws of nature.

From this point of view, Ley argues, Ibn Sīnā defended the real meaning of Aristotle more successfully than the European Scholastic thinkers of the feudal period did. Ibn Sīnā brought out the materialist side of Aristotle’s teaching on matter and form.

Medieval Scholasticism, especially Thomas Aquinas, treated Aristotle as an idealist dualist because he separated form from matter. Yet in the Metaphysics, or First Philosophy, Aristotle had criticized Plato’s “Ideas,” or Forms, and he developed this opposition to Plato in many of his other works as well.
Ibn Sīnā drew a further conclusion. If Aristotle accepted that matter and form are united in the things human beings produce, then this unity must also exist in nature.
Ley argues that this conclusion makes Ibn Sīnā a materialist. The same tendency can also be seen in the way Ibn Sīnā deals with questions on which Aristotle himself moves toward idealism.

These examples show the main direction taken by Marxist studies of Arab-Islamic philosophy. We find many similar examples among Marxist scholars and Orientalists elsewhere in Eastern Europe, as well as in Western Europe and other countries.

Naturally, these scholars differ in their interpretations, perspectives, and methods. They also differ in how familiar they are with the original sources of Arab-Islamic philosophy, how well they understand the texts, and how deeply they can penetrate the traditional forms of expression used in them.

Sometimes these differences may also come from something we discussed earlier: scholars differ in their ability to bring theory and practice together creatively when applying a method to a specific historical case.

What matters most to us here, however, is that the various Marxist studies of the heritage broadly agree with the progressive and democratic direction of the Arab liberation movement at its present stage of development, and with the ideology of the leading forces within that movement.

This comes after a period in which Western Orientalist studies had almost complete control over the study of the heritage. Most of those studies either conflict directly with this progressive line or stand opposed to it, while fitting instead with a current of Arab bourgeois thought that resists and obstructs the development of the Arab movement for liberation and progress.
From what we have seen so far, two different realities emerge in the study of the intellectual heritage of Arab history.
The first is negative: studies that distorted this heritage and either failed to recognize or deliberately ignored its progressive content.
The second is positive: studies that begin from materialist positions, along with studies shaped by movements of liberation.
Both kinds of positive study have helped correct unscientific attitudes toward our intellectual heritage in general and our philosophical heritage in particular.

But one problem remains. We still do not have a study that deals comprehensively with this heritage as a whole and follows it through its historical movement: its origins, growth, and development. Such a study would connect each stage with the development of economic and social relations and with the corresponding material and intellectual development of Arab-Islamic society, all within a world dominated by religious thought and Islamic institutions.

Because existing studies have not done this, they have not been able to bring out all the progressive content and materialist tendencies contained within the heritage across the full course of its development. Nor have they been able to define its different stages in their historical and logical sequence, or to show their complex relationship with the different stages through which religious thought itself developed.

We therefore need a comprehensive study—or several studies—built on this basis. Such work must try to understand the heritage as a connected whole, follow the links and sequence between its stages, and examine its basic problems. Only then can we bring out the other, concrete side of what this heritage contains.
The author of this book has no illusion that he can provide the study we need in anything like its complete form, or even meet all its most important requirements.
Such a task would be extremely difficult for one person even if that person had all the necessary resources. It is harder still when an individual effort lacks many of them.
The truth, then, is that this book is little more than an attempt—almost an adventure.

An undertaking of this importance, on a road that has barely been opened, will inevitably stumble over its own weaknesses and mistakes, perhaps even more often than it encounters the difficulties and challenges of the road itself.

This book is one attempt to respond to the present need for a fully historical study of the heritage. It is also an extended experiment in applying the materialist conception of history to this field.
Its main tasks can be set out as follows:

To study Arab-Islamic philosophy as the product of a historical process within the development of Arab thought itself, and as something connected with the development of Arab-Islamic society during the Middle Ages.
In other words, this philosophy did not arise simply from a single outside influence, as has sometimes been claimed—namely, the borrowing of the philosophies of the East and of the Greek West.

To uncover what some studies have neglected or hidden, and what others have revealed only partly: the progressive values and materialist tendencies contained within the philosophical heritage, such as those discussed earlier in this introduction.

At the same time, we must remember that these values and tendencies appeared in forms shaped by their own historical period. They therefore differ from the forms taken by progressive values and materialist tendencies in our own age, as we explained earlier in some detail.
This is an objective question, not a subjective one.

A qualitative change in social relations, from an earlier form to a higher one, objectively required the appearance of forms of social consciousness that were themselves more advanced than what had come before.
Our understanding of these needs is therefore based on material conditions.

In practical terms, the new and developing relations of production created a need for new knowledge of nature—knowledge capable of meeting the needs created by the development of material social activity.
That knowledge, in turn, developed dialectically as it became more closely connected in practice with those needs.
The development of the natural sciences necessarily leads to a deeper understanding of the laws of nature and to a more materialist understanding of the world as a whole.
This explains why materialist tendencies appeared more clearly and at a higher level in Arab-Islamic philosophy than they had in Greek philosophy during its first life in antiquity.
This is precisely what we meant when we said that Greek philosophy, through its interaction with Arab-Islamic philosophy, acquired a new life—that is, a new stage of development.
